findings.title: Client-side upload size validation ignores site settings, hardcodes 10MB for both images and attachments
findings.body: The check previously used Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so images were validated against max_image_size_kb and attachments against max_attachment_size_kb. The change replaces this with a hardcoded 10MB regardless of type. For attachments this breaks validation in both directions: a site that configured max_attachment_size_kb below 10MB will let users select files the server will reject after upload, and a site that configured a limit above 10MB will now hard-block legitimate attachment uploads on the client. The configured limits should still drive validation (or at least attachments should keep using max_attachment_size_kb).

findings.title: 413 error message now always claims a 10MB limit
findings.body: The 'entity too large' handler previously displayed Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb in the file_too_large message; it now hardcodes 10MB. Whenever the actual configured upload limit (or the web server's limit, which is what typically produces a 413) differs from 10MB, the user is shown a wrong maximum size in the error dialog.

findings.title: API URL download limit hardcoded to 10MB, ignoring max_image_size_kb
findings.body: FileHelper.download for API URL uploads was limited to SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes and is now hardcoded to 10.megabytes. On sites with a configured image limit above 10MB, API uploads via URL that were previously accepted will now silently fail (tempfile is nil after the rescue). The server-side limit should remain consistent with the site setting rather than a magic constant.

findings.title: Downsize is passed an extensionless tempfile path, so ImageMagick cannot determine the output format
findings.body: For regular browser uploads, tempfile is the Rack multipart tempfile (e.g. /tmp/RackMultipart2014...), whose path has no file extension. OptimizedImage.downsize shells out to `convert <from>[0] ... <to>` and ImageMagick derives the output image format from the destination filename extension; with no extension the convert command fails, convert_with returns false, the retry loop spins 5 times, and the oversized file is uploaded unchanged — the feature does nothing for the primary upload path. The same missing extension also means the `from =~ /\.GIF$/i` check in OptimizedImage.optimize never matches, so the animated-gifsicle branch is dead for direct uploads. A temp file carrying the original extension should be used.

findings.title: Oversized animated GIFs are silently de-animated during downsize
findings.body: The downsize instructions use `convert #{from}[0]`, which takes only the first frame, unless the animated branch is chosen. The animated branch is gated on allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails — a setting meant for thumbnails, not originals — and on the source path ending in .GIF, which is never true for direct uploads (see the extensionless tempfile issue). The result is that a user uploading an animated GIF larger than max_image_size_kb gets a static first frame stored as their original image with no warning, destroying the animation.

findings.title: In-place downsize can leave a truncated file that is then uploaded
findings.body: convert is run with the same path as input and output, and the loop only re-checks tempfile.size. If a convert run fails partway through writing the destination, the file can be left truncated/corrupted with a smaller size; the loop condition then passes and Upload.create_for stores the corrupt file as the user's upload. The result of OptimizedImage.downsize is never checked before continuing.

findings.title: Duplicate definition of OptimizedImage.downsize shadows the width/height signature
findings.body: The file now defines self.downsize twice: once at lines 145-147 as downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts) and again at lines 149-151 as downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts). In Ruby the second definition wins, so the four-argument version at line 145 is dead code and any existing caller that passes max_width/max_height will now raise ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments), with Ruby also emitting a 'method redefined' warning. The old definition should have been removed instead of adding an overload.

findings.title: Animated downsize reuses gifsicle --resize-fit, which does not accept a percentage like "80%"
findings.body: downsize_instructions_animated delegates to resize_instructions_animated, which builds `gifsicle --resize-fit #{dimensions}`. gifsicle's --resize-fit expects WxH pixel dimensions; when the new upload downsize code passes "80%", gifsicle will fail, convert_with returns false, and the animated GIF is never downsized. A scale factor (gifsicle --scale) or explicit dimensions are needed for percentage-based downsizing.
